title: PostgreSQL RETURNING Old Value: UPDATE Before and After (PG 18)
description: Get the old value in a PostgreSQL UPDATE with RETURNING old and new (PostgreSQL 18). Examples for UPDATE, upsert, DELETE and MERGE with real output.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: 6.4 Returning Data from Modified Rows

reviewNotes: Regular (Saturday) article, not a series part. Tested on PostgreSQL 18.6 (Ubuntu 18.6-1.pgdg24.04+2) from the PGDG repository on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS; followed the PostgreSQL 18 documentation (docs/current pages in sources) and the 17/18 release notes. All outputs are real and come from one run in article order on a fresh scratch database. Timestamps in the trigger example will differ for readers. SANDBOX CAVEATS: (1) As in earlier runs, postgresql-18 needs liburing2 from archive.ubuntu.com, which is blocked here; I installed a stub liburing.so.2 (only io_method=io_uring would use it; the default is worker). (2) The 'missing FROM-clause entry for table "old"' error for older versions was captured on PostgreSQL 16.15 (the image's distribution package), not 17; the article says '17 or older' and shows it as 'the real error from PostgreSQL 16'. EDITOR CHECKS: (a) The claim that an existing FROM alias named old keeps precedence over the special old row is from my test on 18.6 (shown in the article); the docs only say the aliases can be renamed to avoid conflicts. (b) The table of NULL old/new values for MERGE comes from the tested output; the MERGE page states the unqualified defaults but not NULLs explicitly. (c) The two-session concurrency example was run with two real psql sessions; the explanation follows the Read Committed section of transaction-iso.html. Related links point to the live upsert, SKIP LOCKED and DBA Part 11 articles. Overlap note: the upsert draft mentions RETURNING old/new in one line only; this article covers it fully and links there.

data.text: In PostgreSQL 18 you can get the old value of a row straight from an UPDATE: write RETURNING old.price, new.price and the statement returns the value before the change and the value after it, in one round trip. Before PostgreSQL 18, RETURNING in an UPDATE could only show the new values, so you needed a self-join, a trigger or a separate SELECT to see what was there before.

The same old and new names work in INSERT, DELETE and MERGE. This tutorial shows each one on a small products table, with the real output from PostgreSQL 18, and covers the mistakes that catch people the first time: NULLs where they did not expect them, alias clashes and permissions.
How RETURNING old and new works

RETURNING turns a data-changing statement into something that also returns rows, like a SELECT. Its list accepts the same things a SELECT list does: column names, expressions, * and aliases. It returns one row for each row the statement actually changed.

PostgreSQL 18 adds two special names inside that list. old is the row as it was before the statement changed it, and new is the row after the change. You can write old.column_name, new.column_name, old.* or new.*, and mix them with any expression.
What you get without a prefix did not change. The table below shows the default for each statement and when old or new is NULL.

content: NULL (except rows updated by ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE)
NULL (except when an ON DELETE rule runs an INSERT or UPDATE instead)
new row for INSERT/UPDATE, old row for DELETE

data.text: Think of old and new as the before and after photos of each changed row. PostgreSQL already has both photos while it runs the statement, so returning them costs nothing extra.
This is new in PostgreSQL 18. On PostgreSQL 17 and older, old and new are not special inside RETURNING, so a query using them fails. The section on common mistakes shows the error.
Sample setup
Create a scratch database and a small products table. Every example below runs against this table in order, so the outputs build on each other.

data.caption: Create and fill the products table

data.code:
product_id |        name         |  price  | stock
------------+---------------------+---------+-------
          1 | USB-C cable         |  299.00 |    40
          2 | Wireless mouse      |  799.00 |    15
          3 | Laptop stand        | 1499.00 |     3
          4 | Mechanical keyboard | 3499.00 |     0
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: UPDATE RETURNING before PostgreSQL 18
Say you want to raise every price under 1,000 by 10% and report what changed. A plain RETURNING only gives you the new price. The BEGIN and ROLLBACK here undo the change so the table stays as it was.

data.caption: Unqualified columns return the new values

data.text: The old prices (299.00 and 799.00) are gone. The usual workaround on older versions was to join the table to a locked copy of itself and return the copy's column:

data.caption: The pre-18 workaround: a self-join with FOR UPDATE

data.text: It works, but it reads the table twice, needs FOR UPDATE so another session cannot change the row between the read and the write, and is easy to get wrong. PostgreSQL 18 removes the need for it.
UPDATE RETURNING old and new values in PostgreSQL 18
Return the price before and after
Now the same price rise, written with old and new. You can also compute with both, here the size of the increase.

data.code:
UPDATE products
   SET price = round(price * 1.10, 2)
 WHERE price < 1000
RETURNING product_id, name,
          old.price AS old_price,
          new.price AS new_price,
          new.price - old.price AS increase;
data.caption: Old value, new value and the difference in one statement

data.text: One statement, one pass over the table, and both values per row. new.price gives the same result as plain price, but writing it out makes the intent obvious to the next person who reads the query.
Decrease stock safely and see what it was
A common job is taking items out of stock only if enough are left. Put the check in the WHERE clause and return both stock levels:

data.code:
UPDATE products
   SET stock = stock - 2
 WHERE product_id = 3
   AND stock >= 2
RETURNING product_id,
          old.stock AS stock_before,
          new.stock AS stock_after;
data.caption: Take 2 laptop stands out of stock

data.code:
product_id | stock_before | stock_after
------------+--------------+-------------
          3 |            3 |           1
(1 row)

UPDATE 1
data.caption: Output

data.text: Run exactly the same statement a second time. Only 1 is left, so the WHERE clause matches nothing:

data.code:
product_id | stock_before | stock_after
------------+--------------+-------------
(0 rows)

UPDATE 0
data.caption: Output (second run)

data.text: Zero rows back means the order could not be filled. Your application gets the answer and the before and after numbers from the same atomic statement, with no window for another session to sneak in between a read and a write.
What old means when two sessions update the same row

This is the detail that matters most in production. old is the row version your UPDATE actually changed, not the value your session saw when the statement started. To show it, two psql sessions each take 5 USB-C cables (stock 40) at the same time:

data.caption: Two sessions update the same row
Output (Session B, returned after A committed)

data.text: Session B waited for A's row lock. Under the default Read Committed isolation level, once A committed, B checked its WHERE clause again on the updated version of the row and applied its change to that version. So B's old.stock is 35, not 40, and no stock was lost. If you want the background on row versions, see PostgreSQL DBA Part 11: MVCC, xmin/xmax and row visibility.

This is why RETURNING old is safer than a SELECT before the UPDATE. A separate SELECT without FOR UPDATE can return 40 to both sessions, and your log would then say the stock went from 40 to 35 twice.
Write an audit trail with a CTE
Because RETURNING produces rows, you can put the UPDATE in a WITH clause (a common table expression, or CTE) and insert its output into a history table in the same statement.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE price_history (
    history_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    product_id  integer       NOT NULL,
    old_price   numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    new_price   numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    changed_at  timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

WITH changed AS (
    UPDATE products
       SET price = price - 100
     WHERE product_id IN (3, 4)
    RETURNING product_id,
              old.price AS old_price,
              new.price AS new_price
)
INSERT INTO price_history (product_id, old_price, new_price)
SELECT product_id, old_price, new_price
  FROM changed;

SELECT history_id, product_id, old_price, new_price
  FROM price_history
 ORDER BY history_id;
data.caption: Change prices and log every change in one statement

data.text: The update and the log insert are one statement, so they succeed or fail together. For one-off changes like a price list import this is simpler than an audit trigger. Use a trigger instead when every change from every application must be logged, because a CTE only logs the statements that include it.
INSERT ON CONFLICT: was the row inserted or updated?

With an upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), old is NULL for rows that were newly inserted and holds the previous values for rows that hit a conflict and were updated. That gives you a clean way to tell the two apart. The full upsert syntax is covered in PostgreSQL Upsert with ON CONFLICT.

data.code:
INSERT INTO products (product_id, name, price, stock) VALUES
    (2, 'Wireless mouse', 849.00, 25),
    (5, 'HDMI adapter',   599.00, 30)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
   SET price = EXCLUDED.price,
       stock = EXCLUDED.stock
RETURNING product_id,
          (old.product_id IS NULL) AS inserted,
          old.price AS old_price, new.price AS new_price,
          old.stock AS old_stock, new.stock AS new_stock;
data.caption: Upsert and report what happened to each row

data.text: Product 2 already existed, so it was updated and old shows its earlier price and stock. Product 5 is new, so every old column is NULL. Test old on a NOT NULL column such as the primary key, so a NULL can only mean "no old row". Before PostgreSQL 18 people often checked the system column xmax for this, which relies on internal behaviour; old is the documented way.
With ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, rows that were skipped are not returned at all, because RETURNING only covers rows actually inserted or updated:

data.code:
INSERT INTO products (product_id, name, price, stock) VALUES
    (5, 'HDMI adapter', 650.00, 10),
    (6, 'Webcam',      2199.00,  8)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING product_id, old.price AS old_price, new.price AS new_price;
data.caption: DO NOTHING returns only the inserted rows

data.text: Product 5 was skipped and does not appear. Product 6 was inserted, so its old price is NULL.
DELETE RETURNING old values
For DELETE, unqualified columns already return the deleted row, so old.name and name give the same thing. new is NULL for a plain delete:

data.caption: Delete a row and return what was removed

data.text: Writing old. on a DELETE is optional, but it keeps queries consistent when you copy the same RETURNING list between statements.
MERGE RETURNING with merge_action()

MERGE can insert, update and delete in one statement, so this is where old and new help most. RETURNING on MERGE arrived in PostgreSQL 17, and old/new in 18. The function merge_action() returns 'INSERT', 'UPDATE' or 'DELETE' for each row and can only be used in the RETURNING list of a MERGE.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE stock_feed (
    product_id  integer PRIMARY KEY,
    name        text,
    price       numeric(10,2),
    stock       integer
);

INSERT INTO stock_feed VALUES
    (1, 'USB-C cable',          349.00, 60),
    (4, 'Mechanical keyboard', 3399.00,  0),
    (7, 'Laptop sleeve',        899.00, 12);

MERGE INTO products AS p
USING stock_feed AS f
   ON p.product_id = f.product_id
WHEN MATCHED AND f.stock = 0 THEN
    DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET price = f.price, stock = f.stock
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (product_id, name, price, stock)
    VALUES (f.product_id, f.name, f.price, f.stock)
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, f.product_id,
          old.price AS old_price, new.price AS new_price,
          old.stock AS old_stock, new.stock AS new_stock;
data.caption: Sync products from a supplier feed and report each action

data.text: Each row tells its own story: product 1 was updated (stock 30 after the two sessions earlier, now 60), product 4 was deleted because the feed says 0 in stock, so it has no new values, and product 7 was inserted, so it has no old values.
Renaming old and new with WITH (OLD AS ..., NEW AS ...)
If old or new would clash with a name already in your query, rename them with RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n). Short aliases are also handy for o.*, n.*:

data.code:
UPDATE products
   SET stock = stock + 5
 WHERE product_id = 7
RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n) o.*, n.*;
data.caption: Return the whole row before and after

data.text: Once you give an alias, the names old and new are hidden for that statement. Using them anyway fails:

data.code:
UPDATE products
   SET stock = stock + 5
 WHERE product_id = 7
RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n) old.stock;
data.caption: old is hidden after it is renamed
Output

data.text: What about queries written before PostgreSQL 18 that already use a table or subquery alias called old, like the self-join workaround with AS old instead of AS before? In our test on PostgreSQL 18.6, that alias still won: old.price kept referring to the subquery, so existing queries did not change meaning. To use the new feature in such a query, rename the special rows:

data.code:
BEGIN;
UPDATE products AS p
   SET price = round(p.price * 1.10, 2)
  FROM (SELECT product_id, price
          FROM products
         WHERE product_id = 1
           FOR UPDATE) AS old
 WHERE p.product_id = old.product_id
RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n)
          p.product_id,
          old.price AS from_subquery,
          o.price   AS old_price,
          n.price   AS new_price;
ROLLBACK;
data.caption: An existing alias named old, plus the renamed old row

data.text: RETURNING old and new with triggers
If a BEFORE trigger changes the row, new shows the row as the trigger left it. A typical example is an updated_at column set by a trigger:

data.caption: new includes the value written by the trigger

data.text: The UPDATE never mentioned updated_at, yet new.updated_at holds the trigger's value, and old.updated_at shows when the row was last touched. Your timestamps will differ.
Common mistakes
Running it on PostgreSQL 17 or older
Before PostgreSQL 18, old inside RETURNING is just an unknown table name. This is the real error from PostgreSQL 16:

data.code:
ERROR:  missing FROM-clause entry for table "old"
LINE 1: ...PDATE t SET price = 328.90 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING old.price,...
                                                             ^
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: check SELECT version(); on every server the code runs on, including replicas and test databases. Until all of them are on 18, use the self-join with FOR UPDATE shown earlier.
Expecting old values from a plain INSERT
old.* is always NULL for rows a plain INSERT creates, and new.* is always NULL for a plain DELETE. That is by design, not a bug. Use old on INSERT only with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
Expecting skipped rows from ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
Rows skipped by DO NOTHING, or by a DO UPDATE ... WHERE condition that is false, are not returned. If you need to know which input rows were skipped, compare the returned keys with your input list.
Testing a nullable column to detect inserts
old.discount IS NULL is true both for a new row and for an existing row whose discount was NULL. Test a NOT NULL column, ideally the primary key.
permission denied for table
RETURNING needs SELECT privilege on every column it mentions, through old or new. A role that has UPDATE (stock) and SELECT (product_id, stock) can return old.stock, but adding old.price fails:

data.code: ERROR:  permission denied for table products
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: grant SELECT on the extra columns, or return only the columns the role may read.
Performance and best practices

items.content: Prefer RETURNING old over a SELECT followed by an UPDATE: one statement, one round trip, and the old value is the exact row version you changed.
Return only the columns you need. o.*, n.* is fine in psql, but for wide tables with large text or JSON columns it sends a lot of data back to the application.
Remember RETURNING returns a row for every changed row. An unbounded UPDATE ... RETURNING on millions of rows sends millions of rows to the client; batch large changes.
Name your output columns (AS old_price, AS new_price). Without aliases, old.price and new.price both come back as a column called price, which is confusing in application code.
For queue-style work that claims rows, combine this with the pattern in PostgreSQL FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so workers do not wait on each other.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
How do I get the old value in a PostgreSQL UPDATE?

On PostgreSQL 18, add RETURNING old.column_name to the UPDATE. On older versions, join the table to a subquery that selects the old values with FOR UPDATE and return the subquery's columns, or capture OLD in a row-level trigger.
Does PostgreSQL 17 support RETURNING old and new?
No. PostgreSQL 17 added RETURNING to MERGE, but the old and new names in RETURNING are new in PostgreSQL 18 and work in INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE.
How can I tell if an upsert inserted or updated a row?
On PostgreSQL 18, return (old.primary_key_column IS NULL) AS inserted. It is true for new rows and false for rows updated through ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
Is the old value the one my transaction saw at the start?

Not always. Under Read Committed, if another session updated and committed the row first, your UPDATE applies to that newer version, and old shows the newer version. That is what you want for logging, because it is what your statement actually replaced.
Summary

items.content: RETURNING old.col, new.col returns before and after values; new in PostgreSQL 18.
Works in INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE; unqualified columns keep their old meaning.
old is NULL for inserted rows, new is NULL for deleted rows.
Use old.primary_key IS NULL to tell inserts from updates in an upsert.
old is the row version actually updated, even after waiting for another session.
Rename with RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n) when names clash; then old and new are hidden.
Combine with a CTE to write audit rows in the same statement.
RETURNING needs SELECT privilege on every column it returns.

linkedin.post:
Your UPDATE changed the stock. Now someone asks what it was before, and the old value is gone.

PostgreSQL 18 fixes this with old and new inside RETURNING:

→ UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 2 RETURNING old.stock, new.stock
→ One statement, one round trip, no self-join or extra SELECT
→ In an upsert, old is NULL for inserted rows, so (old.product_id IS NULL) tells you inserted vs updated
→ In MERGE, combine it with merge_action() to see INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE plus both values per row
→ old is the row version your statement actually replaced, even if it waited for another session first

Two traps: on PostgreSQL 17 or older it fails with "missing FROM-clause entry for table old", and after RETURNING WITH (OLD AS o, NEW AS n) the names old and new are hidden.

How do you capture before and after values today: triggers, a SELECT first, or a self-join?

Full tutorial with examples: link in the first comment.
